d.g: Of, relating to, or resembling air or other gases
Of or relating to pneumatics
Powered by, or filled with, compressed air
Having cavities filled with air

pneumatic.e: From Latin pneumaticus, from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “to blow, breath”).

d.g: Of, pertaining to or caused by a pneumococcus bacterium

pneumococcal.e: English pneumococcus Proto-Indo-European *h₂el-der.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. Old French -albor. ▲ Latin -ālis Old French -elbor. ▲ Latin -ālisbor. Middle English -al English -al English pneumococcal From pneumococcus + -al.

d.g: Of or pertaining to the lungs and the stomach
vagus (attributive)

The pneumogastric nerve; one of the tenth pair of cranial nerves which are distributed to the pharynx, esophagus, larynx, lungs, heart, stomach, liver, and spleen, and, in fishes and many amphibia, to the branchial apparatus and also to the sides of the body.
Of, or relating to the lungs; pulmonary.
Of, or relating to pneumonia.
One who has pneumonia.
A medicine to treat lung disease.

pneumonic.e: From the post-Classical Latin pneumonicus and its etymon, the Ancient Greek πνευμονικός (pneumonikós).

d.g: In a pneumatic manner.
Using pneumatics.
d.x: Sand is applied pneumatically to all wheels by the operation of an electro-pneumatic valve at each driving position.

pneumatically.e: English pneumatic Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. Old French -albor. ▲ Latin -ālis Old French -elbor. ▲ Latin -ālisbor. Middle English -al Middle English -ly Middle English -ally English -ally English pneumatically From pneumatic + -ally.

d.g: The branch of mechanics that deals with the mechanical properties of gases
A gas-filled sac or float of some colonial marine coelenterates, such as the Portuguese man-of-war.
An aerial root, in mangroves etc., specialized for gaseous exchange.
An apparatus consisting of a bag with a tube and mouthpiece, which may be attached to the body. The bag contains oxygen to be breathed by the wearer in rescue work in mines, etc.
A gram-positive bacterium, Streptococcus pneumoniae, that causes pneumonia and other infectious diseases
A disease of the lungs caused by inhalation of particulate matter.

pneumoconiosis.e: Alteration of pneumonoconiosis, after pneumo- (“lung”). Compare French pneumoconiose. By surface analysis, pneumo- + coniosis (“disease caused by the inhalation of dust”).

d.g: pneumonia in people with impaired immune systems (typically as a result of AIDS)
An image produced by means of pneumoencephalography.
The surgical removal of all or part of a lung.
d.x: Evarts Graham [...] pioneered the pneumonectomy (the resection of the lung to remove tumors).

pneumonectomy.e: Proto-Indo-European *plew- Proto-Indo-European *-mṓ Proto-Indo-European *pléwmō Ancient Greek πλεύμων (pleúmōn) ▲ Ancient Greek πνέω (pnéō)influ. ▲ Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma)influ. Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn) Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der. Latin -o-bor. …

d.g: Inflammation of the lungs caused by viruses, bacteria or other infectious microorganisms.
d.x: He had always been remarkably immune from such little ailments, and had only once in his life been ill, of a vicious pneumonia long ago at school.

pneumonia.e: From Ancient Greek πνευμονία (pneumonía, “lung disease”), from πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”) + -ία (-ía).

d.g: Inflammation of the tissue of the lungs.
Alternative form of pneumoconiosis.

pneumonoconiosis.e: From German Pneumonokoniosis (1867), from Pneumono- (“lung”) + Ancient Greek κόνις (kónis, “dust”) + German -osis (“disease”). In the earliest attestation (1878), after French pneumonokoniose (1878 or earlier). By surface analysis, pneumono- (“lung”) + coniosis (“disease caused by the inhalation of dust”).

d.g: Presence of air inside the pleural cavity, usually caused by injury either to the lung or the chest wall.

pneumothorax.e: Proto-Indo-European *plew- Proto-Indo-European *-mṓ Proto-Indo-European *pléwmō Ancient Greek πλεύμων (pleúmōn) ▲ Ancient Greek πνέω (pnéō)influ. ▲ Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma)influ. Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn)bor. English pneumo- English thorax English pneumothorax From pneumo- + thorax.

d.g: A pneumococcal vaccine
